title: COMPASS: SRAM-Based Computing-in-Memory SNN Accelerator with Adaptive Spike Speculation
problem: SNNs suffer from low energy efficiency and high latency when using complex neuron models, and exploiting spike sparsity in CIM architectures is challenging due to irregular and time-dependent spike patterns that are difficult to parallelize.
motivation: SNNs are energy-efficient alternatives to DNNs for edge deployment, requiring specialized hardware acceleration to achieve practical performance.
method: COMPASS works by predicting which neurons will fire (spike speculation) based on patterns in recent spike activity, so the hardware can skip unnecessary computation during quiet periods. The system uses SRAM memory that performs neural calculations directly within itself (computing-in-memory), modified with minimal additional circuits to detect and exploit these spike patterns. It reorganizes how data flows through the chip to represent spikes as time-stamped events rather than full arrays, which uses less memory and allows many accumulate-and-compare operations (adding up signals and deciding if neurons fire) to run in parallel.
key_novelty: The core idea is adaptive spike prediction—forecasting which neurons will fire based on patterns—to skip unnecessary calculations in memory-based neural chips while adding almost no hardware cost.
contributions: Efficient speculation-based method to exploit irregular sparsity for both explicit input and implicit output spikes
Modified SRAM-based CIM architecture for dynamic spike pattern generation and exploitation with minimal overhead
Adaptive dataflow with temporal spike representation enabling parallel execution and reduced memory footprint
Achieves 26.7x speedup and 386.7x energy reduction over recent SNN accelerators
primary_theme: SNN acceleration via adaptive spike speculation in SRAM-based CIM
